Adorbs
uh-DORBZ
adjective (Millennial slang)
A clipped, playful form of adorable, built on the same pattern as totes (totally), obvi (obviously), and amazeballs. It appears online in the late 2000s and peaked about 2012–2014; Oxford Dictionaries Online added it in 2014, to widespread grumbling. Used for babies, puppies, couples, outfits, and anything small and sweet, often in a deliberately baby-talk register.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Adorbs is adorable in baby-talk: "That puppy is adorbs." It is a harmless, affectionate word, mostly used by young women about small, sweet things. The Christian observation is less a correction than a curiosity, because the root word has travelled a long way down. In Webster’s 1828 dictionary, adorable meant first "That ought to be adored; worthy of divine honors," and only "in popular use" something worthy of great love. The word for what only God deserves became the word for a kitten in a teacup. Scripture reserves adoration for God: "O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the LORD our maker" (Psa 95:6). When John fell at an angel’s feet, he was stopped: "See thou do it not … worship God" (Rev 19:10). None of this means a Christian cannot call a baby adorable; delight in small, lovely things is a gift, and the Lord Himself took little children in His arms and blessed them (Mar 10:16). It does mean that a careful Christian notices what our words have lost. A father can let his daughter say "adorbs" about the puppy and also teach her the old meaning, so that when she sings "O come, let us adore Him" at Christmas she knows what the word was made for. "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above" (Jas 1:17), including the puppy.

Webster 1828 Definition

Millennial clipped slang (late 2000s; Oxford online 2014) for adorable, cute; harmless, though its root once meant "worthy of divine honors," a reminder that adoration belongs to God (Psa 95:6).

expand to see more

ADORBS, adj. (Millennial slang, late 2000s–2010s; clipped from adorable) Cute, sweet, charming. "Those tiny shoes are adorbs." Same pattern: totes, obvi, amazeballs.

Webster (1828), root adorable: ADORABLE, adjective That ought to be adored; worthy of divine honors. In popular use, worthy of the utmost love or respect.

Decode for parents: harmless; a teaching moment for what "adore" first meant.

Key Scripture

Psa 95:6 — "O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the LORD our maker."

Rev 19:10 — "And I fell at his feet to worship him. And he said unto me, See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus: worship God: for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy."

Mar 10:16 — "And he took them up in his arms, put his hands upon them, and blessed them."

Jas 1:17 — "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning."

Psa 104:24 — "O LORD, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all: the earth is full of thy riches."

Modern Corruption

Adorbs is harmless affection; its only lesson is the drift of its root, from "worthy of divine honors" to "cute," which reminds us to keep adoration for God.

expand to see more

If there is a corruption here, it belongs to the root, not the slang. Adorable fell from a word of worship to a word for cuteness long before Millennials clipped it. The drift is typical of a culture that spends its highest words on its smallest pleasures, so that language for God has to compete with language for brunch. Children who never hear the old meaning will not miss it, and they will sing "adore" in carols without feeling its weight.

The redemption is twofold. Enjoy the small sweet things, because they are God’s gifts: "O LORD, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all" (Psa 104:24). And keep a vocabulary of worship strong enough for worship. Teach the young to delight in puppies and babies, and to bow their knees to the only One who is truly adorable in the 1828 sense.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin adorare (to speak to, to worship) → adorable (worthy of divine honors; popularly, lovable) → late-2000s clipped adorbs → Oxford online 2014.

expand to see more

Latin ad + orare — to speak to, to pray to; adorare — to worship

17th c.: adorable — worthy of divine honors; later, popularly, delightful

Late 2000s: clipped adorbs, with totes, obvi

2014: added to Oxford Dictionaries Online

Biblical anchor: O come, let us worship and bow down (Psa 95:6); worship God (Rev 19:10)

Usage

""Her baby in the little bear hat is adorbs.""

"Every good gift is from above (Jas 1:17), the puppy included."

"Adore in the old sense only One: let us kneel before the LORD our maker (Psa 95:6)."
